title: Trump admin still won't let Wi-Fi giant TP-Link sell its latest routers in US
gist: Under the Trump administration's March 2026 ban on foreign-made consumer routers (via the FCC Covered List), TP-Link has failed to win a conditional-approval waiver, blocking US sales of its new Wi-Fi 8 routers, while 26 waivers have gone to rivals including Starlink, Amazon/Eero, Netgear and Asus. The opaque waiver process, category-wide Covered List additions (routers, drones, robots, inverters), state AG lawsuits and FCC power-limit findings stack against TP-Link, and bipartisan House legislation seeks to rein in category bans.

insights.claim: Since March 2026 the US bars import or sale of any new consumer router model manufactured, assembled, designed or developed outside the US unless the maker obtains a conditional-approval waiver reviewed by the FCC, DoD and DHS.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Router market access is now a political licence; US networking-hardware share will be redistributed by waiver decisions.
insights.locator: The rules prevent the import or sale

insights.claim: TP-Link has not obtained a waiver, so its newly released Wi-Fi 8 routers (e.g. the Archer 8 Ultra, £899.99 in the UK) cannot be sold in the US, though models approved before March 2026 remain on sale.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: TP-Link's US product line will age out over time, opening next-gen share to waiver holders.
insights.locator: While some of its competitors have obtained exemptions

insights.claim: 26 router waivers have been issued, including to SpaceX's Starlink and to Amazon for its Leo satellite service and Eero devices, plus Netgear, Asus, Adtran, Calix, Nokia, Micro-Star International, Askey, Zyxel, Humax and Vantiva.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Waiver holders like Netgear, Calix and Adtran are positioned to take US retail/ISP router share from TP-Link.
insights.locator: Companies led by Trump allies Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos

insights.claim: The waiver review is secretive enough that outsiders cannot tell whether consistent security criteria are applied or waivers favor politically connected firms; companies led by Trump allies Musk and Bezos fared well.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Political proximity may be a material factor in US market access for hardware vendors — a governance risk to price in.
insights.quote: Companies led by Trump allies Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos fared well in the reviews.
insights.locator: Companies led by Trump allies Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos

insights.claim: The FCC on November 5 granted cable lobby NCTA's request to relax the router ban so ISPs can more easily change components in their supplied devices.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: ISP-supplied router supply chains got relief, lowering disruption risk for cable operators.
insights.locator: Many home Internet subscribers simply use the router

insights.claim: Router makers seeking conditional approval must disclose country of origin for every component and software element, single-source parts with contingencies, assembly locations, a quantitative country-concentration assessment by value and volume, and a time-bound plan to build US manufacturing.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Compliance burden favors vendors with US manufacturing plans; expect onshoring capex announcements tied to market access.
insights.quote: quantitative assessment of supply chain concentration by country, expressed as both a percentage of total value and production volume
insights.locator: Router makers seeking conditional approvals must submit

insights.claim: TP-Link has offered a nearly $1 billion US investment to equip existing factories and build highly automated plants to assemble Wi-Fi 8 routers in the US as soon as next year, contingent on receiving its waiver.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Market-access-for-investment bargaining is the template; watch whether the administration accepts it.
insights.quote: a nearly $1 billion investment in America

insights.claim: There are no published thresholds for how much US content makes a router 'US-made', and key chipsets come from Qualcomm and Broadcom, leaving vendors unsure what qualifies.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Regulatory ambiguity prolongs waiver timelines; US chip suppliers may benefit from domestic-content framing.
insights.quote: Or what about, we buy our chipsets for these products from Qualcomm and Broadcom. Is that a US product?

insights.claim: An April 2025 Bloomberg report said that aside from Vietnamese-sourced components worth 0.5% of input value, all components in TP-Link's Vietnam-made US routers are imported from China.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Vietnam final assembly does not escape China-origin scrutiny; transshipment-style sourcing is a regulatory vulnerability.
insights.locator: TP-Link says the devices it sells in the US are made in Vietnam

insights.claim: The FCC Covered List, created by a 2020 law, originally named specific companies (Huawei, ZTE, Kaspersky, surveillance makers), but under Trump it now bans whole product categories regardless of vendor, including foreign routers, drones, robotic devices and power inverters.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Category bans extend to robotics and power inverters — relevant to solar/energy storage and robotics supply chains.
insights.locator: For the first few years of the Covered List’s existence

insights.claim: Former FCC and DOJ official Betsy McIntyre argues category-wide Covered List bans muddle a tool meant to name specific risky companies, though some argue such bans usefully force supply-chain scrutiny and onshoring.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Policy debate may shift the list back toward entity-specific bans, reducing blanket import risk.
insights.quote: It’s a little bit muddled now.

insights.claim: A bipartisan House bill from Frank Pallone and Brett Guthrie would limit FCC category bans to foreign-adversary-controlled entities (China, Russia, North Korea, Iran), require a week's notice to Congress, and treat category additions as major rules subject to Congressional Review Act overturn.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: If passed, category bans on routers/drones/inverters become harder to impose and easier to reverse.
insights.locator: The Pallone/Guthrie bill would also require

insights.claim: Drone makers have faced the same FCC import ban since December 2025; DJI sued the FCC in February, and the government's motion to dismiss as 'premature' is pending at the Ninth Circuit, illustrating that litigation against Covered List bans can drag on for years.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Litigation is a slow remedy; banned vendors should be modeled as out of the US market for years.

insights.claim: Former NSA cybersecurity director Rob Joyce testified that TP-Link grew from about 10% to at least 60% of the US retail Wi-Fi/SoHo router market since 2019 by apparently pricing below profitability, and its routers were exploited in Volt, Flax and Salt Typhoon attacks.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The national-security narrative around predatory pricing underpins both the ban and the antitrust probe.
insights.quote: They appear to be selling at price points below profitability to drive out the western competition

insights.claim: TP-Link disputes dominance claims, citing a 36.6% unit and 31% dollar share of the US consumer router market in 2024, and under 10% of North American residential router sales when ISP-supplied routers are included.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Share depends heavily on whether ISP channel is counted; retail channel exposure to the ban is larger.

insights.claim: Florida and three other Republican-AG states sued TP-Link alleging it misled consumers about China ties, 21 Republican AGs urged the FCC to factor state-law violations into its waiver review, and the FCC tentatively found several existing TP-Link routers, including the Archer BE670, exceeded power limits.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Stacking enforcement actions reduce TP-Link's waiver odds and raise risk of action against already-sold devices.
insights.locator: Florida and three other states with Republican attorneys general

insights.claim: A former FCC Enforcement Bureau deputy chief notes the agency commonly scrutinizes a company's existing equipment compliance when it has significant requests pending, suggesting the power-limit probe is linked to TP-Link's waiver application.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Pending waiver applicants face heightened enforcement exposure — a negative leading indicator for approval.
insights.locator: “Any time a company has significant requests before the agency

insights.claim: Bruce Schneier argues TP-Link routers are no less secure than competitors' because consumer router and IoT economics don't reward security staffing or patching, and nearly all routers are made in China regardless of brand.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Brand-based bans may not materially improve security; IoT security remains structurally underfunded.
insights.quote: The way you patch a lot of your home routers is you throw it away and buy a new one. That’s the patch mechanism.
